# Avery Carnes Trial Lawyers

> Personal injury law firm in metro Atlanta, Georgia, led by two founding partners, Thomas L. "Trey" Carnes III and C. Benjamin "Ben" Avery. Plaintiff side only. Free consultation; no attorney's fee unless the firm recovers money for the client.

Ben Avery started his career at an insurance defense firm, defending personal injury claims, and has tried cases to verdict; he now represents only injured people and families. Trey Carnes represented Georgia hospitals and health systems on third-party reimbursement (medical bills, liens and subrogation) before opening the firm. Every case is handled by an attorney, never only by a paralegal or case manager, and the firm takes a limited number of cases each year.

Cite as: Avery Carnes Trial Lawyers, Atlanta, Georgia — https://avery-carnes.vercel.app/

## Who this is for
People hurt in metro Atlanta by someone else's carelessness, and families who lost someone in a preventable death.

## Services
### Car Accidents
A crash takes seconds. The insurance claim can take months, and the other driver's insurer starts working on it the same day. Get a lawyer on your side who knows how they think. Page: https://avery-carnes.vercel.app/practice-areas/auto-accidents/

### Truck Accidents
A truck crash is not just a bigger car crash. There's a trucking company, its insurer, and federal safety rules, and the company's lawyers often start working the day of the wreck. Page: https://avery-carnes.vercel.app/practice-areas/truck-accidents/

### Motorcycle & Bicycle Accidents
Riders get hurt worse and blamed faster. Trey Carnes started his legal career at a firm that represented injured motorcycle riders. We know the bias you'll face, and how to answer it. Page: https://avery-carnes.vercel.app/practice-areas/motorcycle-bicycle-accidents/

### Wrongful Death
Nothing replaces the person you lost. A wrongful death case can get your family answers, hold the responsible people accountable, and ease the money pressure that follows a loss. Page: https://avery-carnes.vercel.app/practice-areas/wrongful-death/

### Nursing Home Abuse & Neglect
You trusted a facility to care for someone you love. When bedsores, falls, or unexplained injuries show up, you deserve real answers, and the facility should answer for what happened. Page: https://avery-carnes.vercel.app/practice-areas/nursing-home-neglect-or-abuse/

### Product Liability
When a product fails the way it was never supposed to, the company that made it can be responsible. Keep the product, and call us before anyone else asks for it. Page: https://avery-carnes.vercel.app/practice-areas/products-liability/

### Dog Bites
A serious bite can mean surgery, scars and fear that lasts. Georgia law can hold a careless owner responsible, and homeowner's or renter's insurance often pays these claims. Page: https://avery-carnes.vercel.app/practice-areas/dog-bites/

### Catastrophic Injury
Some injuries change everything: work, family, home, the future. A catastrophic injury case has to account for all of it, including care you'll need years from now. Page: https://avery-carnes.vercel.app/practice-areas/catastrophic-injury/

### Slip & Fall
Stores, apartment complexes and other businesses have to keep their property reasonably safe. When they ignore a hazard and someone gets hurt, they can be responsible. Page: https://avery-carnes.vercel.app/practice-areas/slip-and-fall/

## How working with us goes
1. You call or send a message: Tell us what happened. It's free, and there's no obligation.
2. We review your case: We look at the facts and tell you plainly where you stand.
3. We build the case: Reports, records, photos, video, witnesses and every insurance policy that could pay.
4. We push for a fair result: We negotiate from a case that's ready for trial. If the offer isn't fair, we're ready to file.

## Fees
No attorney's fee unless we recover money for you. Whether you owe case costs (such as filing fees or expert fees) if there is no recovery is set out in your written fee agreement.

## Questions people ask
**How much does it cost to hire Avery Carnes?**
Your first consultation is free. We take injury cases on a contingency fee, which means no attorney's fee unless we recover money for you. The fee is a percentage of the recovery, set out in a written agreement you sign before we start. That agreement also explains how case costs, like filing fees and expert fees, are handled.

**How long do I have to file an injury claim in Georgia?**
For most injury claims, Georgia gives you two years from the date of the injury to file a lawsuit (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33). Claims against a government are much shorter: written notice to a city is due within six months (O.C.G.A. § 36-33-5), and to a county or the State within twelve months (O.C.G.A. § 36-11-1 and § 50-21-26). Miss the deadline and the claim can be lost for good.

**What if I was partly at fault?**
Georgia uses a modified comparative fault rule (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33). You can still recover if you were less than 50% at fault, but your award is reduced by your share of the fault. At 50% or more, you recover nothing. Insurers know this, which is why they often try to shift blame onto the injured person.

**Should I give a statement to the other driver's insurance company?**
You do not have to give a recorded statement to the other driver's insurer, and it is usually smart to talk to a lawyer first. Their adjuster's job is to pay as little as possible. Your own policy may require you to cooperate with your own insurer, so read it or ask us.

**Who will actually handle my case?**
An attorney. At Avery Carnes, your case is handled by a lawyer, never only by a paralegal, case manager or intake rep. The firm takes a limited number of cases each year so every client gets personal attention.

**Can you come to me?**
Yes. If you can't come to our office at Perimeter Center, we come to you. Tell us where you are when you call.

**What is my case worth?**
No honest lawyer can give you a number on the first call. What a case is worth depends on the injuries, the medical treatment and bills, lost income, how the injury changes your life, who was at fault, and how much insurance is available. We'll explain each of those for your case and keep you updated as the facts come in.

**What changed in Georgia injury law in 2025?**
Georgia passed a major tort reform law, Senate Bill 68, signed on April 21, 2025. For injuries on or after that date, the defense may show the jury whether you wore a seat belt, and what was actually paid, or is needed to pay, your medical bills, not just what was billed. It also limits how lawyers can suggest dollar amounts for pain and suffering, and in most cases lets either side require a trial to be split into a fault phase and a damages phase. These rules make careful handling of medical bills and evidence more important than ever.

**Where is your office?**
We're in The King Building, 6 Concourse Pkwy #1650, Atlanta, GA 30328, at Perimeter Center near GA-400 and I-285. Call 404-602-0028.

**Which areas do you serve?**
We represent injured people across metro Atlanta, including Fulton County, DeKalb County, Gwinnett County, Cobb County and Sandy Springs. The firm has represented clients in 25 Georgia counties.

**Will my case go to trial?**
Many injury claims settle without a trial. Some don't, and insurers pay attention to which lawyers are ready to try a case. The firm has litigated in Georgia's state and federal courts, and Ben has tried cases to verdict.

**Does it cost anything to call?**
No. The call and the case review are free, and there is no obligation to hire us.

# About Avery Carnes Trial Lawyers

Avery Carnes is an Atlanta personal injury firm. Your case is always handled by an attorney, never only by a paralegal, case manager, customer service rep or investigator. The firm takes a limited number of cases each year.

## Thomas L. Carnes III (Trey Carnes), Founding Partner

Trey graduated from Shorter College and earned his law degree from Mississippi College School of Law in Jackson, Mississippi.

He began his legal career at a boutique firm in Cartersville, Georgia, representing riders hurt in motorcycle crashes.

Before opening his own practice, Trey represented Georgia hospitals and healthcare systems in third-party reimbursement. That work taught him how medical bills, provider liens and subrogation claims (an insurer's right to be paid back out of your recovery) shape what an injured person actually takes home.

He has represented injured people in Georgia, Alabama and Mississippi.

Outside the office, Trey lives in Brookhaven. He plays golf, runs, works on vintage vehicles, and goes to Braves, Falcons and Hawks games with his wife and son.

- Education: Shorter College, Mississippi College School of Law
- Memberships: State Bar of Georgia, American Bar Association, American Association for Justice, Georgia Trial Lawyers Association
- Admitted to practice: U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Georgia; U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Georgia; Supreme Court of Georgia; Court of Appeals of Georgia; All State and Superior Courts in Georgia

## C. Benjamin Avery (Ben Avery), Founding Partner

Ben grew up in Gwinnett County and graduated from Buford High School. He earned his undergraduate degree at the University of Georgia and his law degree from John Marshall Law School.

After law school, Ben joined an insurance defense firm in Athens, Georgia, where he focused only on defending personal injury claims. He gained deep litigation experience there and tried cases to verdict.

He left that work to represent people instead of insurance companies. Today he represents only individuals and families who have been hurt by others.

Ben is an amateur golfer who competes in state and national amateur tournaments. He and his wife, Hannah, have three children: Amy, Will and Caroline.

- Education: University of Georgia, John Marshall Law School
- Memberships: State Bar of Georgia, American Bar Association, American Association for Justice, Georgia Trial Lawyers Association
- Admitted to practice: U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Georgia; U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Georgia; Supreme Court of Georgia; Court of Appeals of Georgia; All State and Superior Courts in Georgia

# Atlanta Car Accident Lawyer

A crash takes seconds. The insurance claim can take months, and the other driver's insurer starts working on it the same day. Get a lawyer on your side who knows how they think.

## Georgia at a glance

- **2 years**: to file most injury lawsuits in Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33)
- **Under 50%**: your share of fault must stay below this to recover (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33)
- **$25,000**: the minimum bodily-injury coverage per person Georgia requires a driver to carry

## What to do after a car accident in Georgia

1. **Get medical care.** Some injuries, like concussions and back injuries, show up hours or days later. A record that starts on day one matters.
2. **Call the police.** Georgia law requires reporting a crash that causes injury, death, or at least $500 in property damage (O.C.G.A. § 40-6-273). Ask for the report number.
3. **Take photos and names.** Vehicles, the road, traffic lights, your injuries, and the names and phone numbers of witnesses.
4. **Don't give a recorded statement** to the other driver's insurer before you talk to a lawyer.
5. **Call us.** Video from businesses and traffic cameras can be recorded over. The sooner we know, the sooner we can ask for it.

## How Georgia law treats your claim

Georgia is an at-fault state. The driver who caused the crash, and their insurance company, are responsible for the harm. You can claim medical bills, lost income, damage to your vehicle, and pain and suffering.

Georgia uses a **modified comparative fault** rule (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33). If you were partly at fault, your award goes down by your share. At 50% or more, you recover nothing. That is why insurers work so hard to put some of the blame on you.

Georgia drivers must carry at least $25,000 per person and $50,000 per crash in bodily-injury coverage. Serious injuries often cost more than that. Your own uninsured/underinsured motorist (UM) coverage may pay the difference, so we look at every policy that could apply.

> **New since 2025.** For crashes on or after April 21, 2025, Georgia's tort reform law (SB 68) lets the defense tell the jury whether you wore a seat belt, and show what was actually paid on your medical bills. That makes how your bills and treatment are documented more important than ever. Trey's earlier work for Georgia hospitals on medical bills, liens and subrogation is directly relevant here.

## What we do in a car accident case

- Get the police report, photos, 911 calls, and any camera footage we can find.
- Find every insurance policy that could pay: the other driver's, their employer's if they were working, and your own UM coverage.
- Track your medical treatment and bills, and deal with health-insurance and hospital liens so more of the recovery reaches you.
- Handle every call with the insurers so you can focus on getting better.
- Prepare the case for trial from the start, so the insurer knows we're ready if a fair offer never comes.

## Questions

### Should I give a statement to the other driver's insurance company?

You do not have to give a recorded statement to the other driver's insurer, and it is usually smart to talk to a lawyer first. Their adjuster's job is to pay as little as possible. Your own policy may require you to cooperate with your own insurer, so read it or ask us.

### What if I was partly at fault?

Georgia uses a modified comparative fault rule (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33). You can still recover if you were less than 50% at fault, but your award is reduced by your share of the fault. At 50% or more, you recover nothing. Insurers know this, which is why they often try to shift blame onto the injured person.

### How long do I have to file an injury claim in Georgia?

For most injury claims, Georgia gives you **two years from the date of the injury** to file a lawsuit (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33). Claims against a government are much shorter: written notice to a city is due within **six months** (O.C.G.A. § 36-33-5), and to a county or the State within **twelve months** (O.C.G.A. § 36-11-1 and § 50-21-26). Miss the deadline and the claim can be lost for good.

### What is my case worth?

No honest lawyer can give you a number on the first call. What a case is worth depends on the injuries, the medical treatment and bills, lost income, how the injury changes your life, who was at fault, and how much insurance is available. We'll explain each of those for your case and keep you updated as the facts come in.

# Atlanta Truck Accident Lawyer

A truck crash is not just a bigger car crash. There's a trucking company, its insurer, and federal safety rules, and the company's lawyers often start working the day of the wreck.

## Georgia at a glance

- **49 C.F.R.**: Parts 390–399: the federal safety rules commercial truck companies must follow
- **Part 395**: limits how long a truck driver may drive before resting (hours of service)
- **2 years**: to file most injury lawsuits in Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33)

## Why truck cases are different

Commercial trucks are governed by federal safety rules (49 C.F.R. Part 382 and Parts 390–399). Those rules cover driver hours, driver qualifications, drug and alcohol testing, and vehicle inspection and maintenance. When a company breaks them, the records usually show it.

More than one party can be responsible: the driver, the trucking company, the company that loaded the cargo, the owner of the trailer, or a maintenance shop. Each may have its own insurance.

## The evidence that matters, and why speed matters

- **Electronic logging device (ELD) data** showing the driver's hours (49 C.F.R. Part 395).
- **Engine and dash camera data** showing speed and braking before the crash.
- **The driver qualification file** and drug and alcohol test results.
- **Inspection and maintenance records** for the truck and trailer.
- **Dispatch and delivery records** that show the schedule the driver was under.

Some of this can be lost or overwritten. One of our first steps is a written demand that the company preserve it.

> **A partner who started on the other side.** Ben started his career at an insurance defense firm, defending injury claims. He knows how a defense team builds its case, because that was his job.

## Where trucks and traffic meet in metro Atlanta

I-285, I-75, I-85, I-20 and GA-400 carry heavy truck traffic through Fulton, DeKalb, Gwinnett and Cobb counties every day, including the I-85/I-285 interchange in DeKalb. We handle crashes on all of them.

## Questions

### How long do I have to file an injury claim in Georgia?

For most injury claims, Georgia gives you **two years from the date of the injury** to file a lawsuit (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33). Claims against a government are much shorter: written notice to a city is due within **six months** (O.C.G.A. § 36-33-5), and to a county or the State within **twelve months** (O.C.G.A. § 36-11-1 and § 50-21-26). Miss the deadline and the claim can be lost for good.

### What if I was partly at fault?

Georgia uses a modified comparative fault rule (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33). You can still recover if you were less than 50% at fault, but your award is reduced by your share of the fault. At 50% or more, you recover nothing. Insurers know this, which is why they often try to shift blame onto the injured person.

### Will my case go to trial?

Many injury claims settle without a trial. Some don't, and insurers pay attention to which lawyers are ready to try a case. The firm has litigated in Georgia's state and federal courts, and Ben has tried cases to verdict.

### What is my case worth?

No honest lawyer can give you a number on the first call. What a case is worth depends on the injuries, the medical treatment and bills, lost income, how the injury changes your life, who was at fault, and how much insurance is available. We'll explain each of those for your case and keep you updated as the facts come in.

# Atlanta Motorcycle & Bicycle Accident Lawyer

Riders get hurt worse and blamed faster. Trey Carnes started his legal career at a firm that represented injured motorcycle riders. We know the bias you'll face, and how to answer it.

## Georgia at a glance

- **Helmets**: Georgia requires every motorcycle rider and passenger to wear one (O.C.G.A. § 40-6-315)
- **3 feet**: the minimum space a driver must keep when passing a bicycle in the same lane (O.C.G.A. § 40-6-56)
- **Under 50%**: your share of fault must stay below this to recover (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33)

## Motorcycle crashes

Many motorcycle crashes happen when a driver turns left across a rider's path or changes lanes without seeing them. Afterward, the insurer often argues the rider was speeding or hard to see. Witnesses, scene photos, vehicle damage and camera footage are how we push back.

Georgia requires helmets for every rider and passenger (O.C.G.A. § 40-6-315). If you weren't wearing one, you may still have a claim. Talk to us before you assume otherwise.

## Bicycle crashes

Georgia law requires a driver passing a bicycle to move into a lane not next to the rider when that is practical. If it isn't possible or safe, the driver must slow down (to 25 mph, or 10 mph under the limit, whichever is greater) and keep at least three feet away while passing (O.C.G.A. § 40-6-56). Cyclists also have the right to use the road. When a driver passes too close, opens a door into a bike lane, or turns across a rider, the driver can be responsible.

## What we do for injured riders

- Get the scene evidence and footage before it's gone.
- Work with your doctors to document injuries that are common in rider crashes: fractures, road rash, head and spinal injuries.
- Deal with hospital bills and liens. Before founding the firm, Trey represented Georgia hospitals on medical bills and liens.
- Look for every policy that could pay, including your own uninsured/underinsured motorist coverage.

## Questions

### What if I was partly at fault?

Georgia uses a modified comparative fault rule (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33). You can still recover if you were less than 50% at fault, but your award is reduced by your share of the fault. At 50% or more, you recover nothing. Insurers know this, which is why they often try to shift blame onto the injured person.

### How long do I have to file an injury claim in Georgia?

For most injury claims, Georgia gives you **two years from the date of the injury** to file a lawsuit (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33). Claims against a government are much shorter: written notice to a city is due within **six months** (O.C.G.A. § 36-33-5), and to a county or the State within **twelve months** (O.C.G.A. § 36-11-1 and § 50-21-26). Miss the deadline and the claim can be lost for good.

### Can you come to me?

Yes. If you can't come to our office at Perimeter Center, we come to you. Tell us where you are when you call.

# Atlanta Wrongful Death Lawyer

Nothing replaces the person you lost. A wrongful death case can get your family answers, hold the responsible people accountable, and ease the money pressure that follows a loss.

## Georgia at a glance

- **2 years**: from the date of death to file in most cases (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33)
- **Full value**: of the life of the person who died is what Georgia law measures (O.C.G.A. § 51-4-1 and 51-4-2)
- **2 claims**: a family's wrongful death claim, plus a separate claim by the estate

## Who can bring a wrongful death claim in Georgia

Georgia law sets the order. The surviving spouse brings the claim first and shares it with any children. If there is no spouse, the children bring it. If there is no spouse or child, the parents may. If none of them survive, the administrator of the estate brings it for the next of kin.

## What the claims cover

Georgia measures a wrongful death claim by the **full value of the life** of the person who died, seen from that person's point of view. That includes the income they would have earned and the parts of life that have no price tag.

The estate can bring a separate claim for medical and funeral expenses, and for the pain and suffering the person went through before death.

## How we work with families

- If you can't come to us, we come to you.
- We handle the insurers, the investigators and the paperwork so your family doesn't have to.
- We explain every step, in plain words, before it happens.
- We prepare the case as if a jury will hear it.

> **Talk to us before you sign anything.** Insurers sometimes contact families early with a release to sign. A release can end the claim for good. Please talk to a lawyer first.

## Questions

### How long do I have to file an injury claim in Georgia?

For most injury claims, Georgia gives you **two years from the date of the injury** to file a lawsuit (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33). Claims against a government are much shorter: written notice to a city is due within **six months** (O.C.G.A. § 36-33-5), and to a county or the State within **twelve months** (O.C.G.A. § 36-11-1 and § 50-21-26). Miss the deadline and the claim can be lost for good.

### How much does it cost to hire Avery Carnes?

The fee is a percentage of the recovery, set out in a written agreement you sign before we start. That agreement also explains how case costs, like filing fees and expert fees, are handled.

### Who will actually handle my case?

An attorney. At Avery Carnes, your case is handled by a lawyer, never only by a paralegal, case manager or intake rep. The firm takes a limited number of cases each year so every client gets personal attention.

### Can you come to me?

Yes. If you can't come to our office at Perimeter Center, we come to you. Tell us where you are when you call.

# Atlanta Nursing Home Abuse & Neglect Lawyer

You trusted a facility to care for someone you love. When bedsores, falls, or unexplained injuries show up, you deserve real answers, and the facility should answer for what happened.

## Georgia at a glance

- **O.C.G.A. § 31-8-100**: and following: Georgia's bill of rights for residents of long-term care facilities
- **2 years**: to file most injury lawsuits in Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33)
- **911**: if someone is in danger right now, call first and ask questions later

## Warning signs families notice

- Bedsores (pressure ulcers), especially ones that get worse
- Falls, broken bones, or bruises no one can explain
- Sudden weight loss, dehydration, or poor hygiene
- Medication mistakes, or a resident who seems over-sedated
- A loved one who becomes withdrawn or afraid of certain staff

## Your loved one's rights

Georgia law gives residents of long-term care facilities a set of rights, including the right to adequate and appropriate care, and to be free from improper restraints and isolation (O.C.G.A. § 31-8-100 and following, including § 31-8-108 and § 31-8-109). Federal rules also apply to facilities that take Medicare or Medicaid.

## What to do now

1. If anyone is in danger, call 911.
2. Take dated photos and write down what you see, who you spoke to, and when.
3. Ask for your loved one's care records in writing.
4. Call us. We can look at the records, find out what went wrong, and explain your options.

> **Experience with medical bills and liens.** Before founding the firm, Trey represented Georgia hospitals and health systems on third-party reimbursement, including medical bills and provider liens.

For most injury claims, Georgia gives you **two years from the date of the injury** to file a lawsuit (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33). Claims against a government are much shorter: written notice to a city is due within **six months** (O.C.G.A. § 36-33-5), and to a county or the State within **twelve months** (O.C.G.A. § 36-11-1 and § 50-21-26). Miss the deadline and the claim can be lost for good.

# Atlanta Product Liability Lawyer

When a product fails the way it was never supposed to, the company that made it can be responsible. Keep the product, and call us before anyone else asks for it.

## Georgia at a glance

- **O.C.G.A. § 51-1-11**: Georgia's product liability law, including strict liability for manufacturers
- **10 years**: the general cut-off for strict liability claims, counted from the product's first sale
- **Keep it**: the product itself is often the most important piece of evidence

## Kinds of product cases

- **Design defects:** the product is dangerous as designed.
- **Manufacturing defects:** something went wrong when this one was made.
- **Warning defects:** the company didn't warn about a danger it knew about.

## How Georgia law works

Under O.C.G.A. § 51-1-11, a manufacturer can be held strictly liable when a product that was not merchantable and reasonably suited to its use causes injury. That means you may not have to prove the company was careless, only that the product was defective and caused the harm.

Georgia also has a statute of repose: strict liability claims generally must be brought within 10 years of the product's first sale. Some negligence claims can be brought later, including claims that a manufacturer failed to warn about a danger it learned of, and claims about products that cause disease or birth defects. Timing matters, so call early.

## What to do now

1. Keep the product, the packaging, the manual and the receipt. Don't repair or throw anything away.
2. Take photos of the product and your injuries.
3. Don't send the product back to the company before you talk to us.
4. Call us for a free case review.

## Questions

### How much does it cost to hire Avery Carnes?

Your first consultation is free. We take injury cases on a contingency fee, which means **no attorney's fee unless we recover money for you**. The fee is a percentage of the recovery, set out in a written agreement you sign before we start. That agreement also explains how case costs, like filing fees and expert fees, are handled.

### What is my case worth?

No honest lawyer can give you a number on the first call. What a case is worth depends on the injuries, the medical treatment and bills, lost income, how the injury changes your life, who was at fault, and how much insurance is available. We'll explain each of those for your case and keep you updated as the facts come in.

### Will my case go to trial?

Many injury claims settle without a trial. Some don't, and insurers pay attention to which lawyers are ready to try a case. The firm has litigated in Georgia's state and federal courts, and Ben has tried cases to verdict.

### Does it cost anything to call?

No. The call and the case review are free, and there is no obligation to hire us.

# Atlanta Dog Bite Lawyer

A serious bite can mean surgery, scars and fear that lasts. Georgia law can hold a careless owner responsible, and homeowner's or renter's insurance often pays these claims.

## Georgia at a glance

- **O.C.G.A. § 51-2-7**: Georgia's dog bite law
- **Leash laws**: breaking a local leash law can help show an owner is responsible
- **2 years**: to file most injury lawsuits in Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33)

## When is a dog owner responsible in Georgia?

Under O.C.G.A. § 51-2-7, an owner can be liable when the dog is vicious or dangerous and the owner carelessly manages it or lets it go at large, and the person bitten did not provoke it. If the dog was off its leash where a local law required one, that can help show the dog was dangerous.

## What to do after a dog bite

1. Get medical care. Bites can get infected, and a doctor's record matters.
2. Get the owner's name, address and insurance, and the dog's vaccination records.
3. Report the bite to local animal control.
4. Take photos of the injury as it heals, and of where the bite happened.
5. Call us before you talk to the owner's insurance company.

## Who pays

Many dog bite claims are paid by the owner's homeowner's or renter's insurance, not out of the owner's pocket. We find the policy and deal with the insurer.

Your first consultation is free. We take injury cases on a contingency fee, which means **no attorney's fee unless we recover money for you**. The fee is a percentage of the recovery, set out in a written agreement you sign before we start. That agreement also explains how case costs, like filing fees and expert fees, are handled.

### How long do I have to file an injury claim in Georgia?

For most injury claims, Georgia gives you **two years from the date of the injury** to file a lawsuit (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33). Claims against a government are much shorter: written notice to a city is due within **six months** (O.C.G.A. § 36-33-5), and to a county or the State within **twelve months** (O.C.G.A. § 36-11-1 and § 50-21-26). Miss the deadline and the claim can be lost for good.

# Atlanta Catastrophic Injury Lawyer

Some injuries change everything: work, family, home, the future. A catastrophic injury case has to account for all of it, including care you'll need years from now.

## Georgia at a glance

- **Lifetime**: future medical care and lost earning power are part of the claim
- **Liens**: health insurers and hospitals may claim part of a recovery; we deal with them
- **2 years**: to file most injury lawsuits in Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33)

## What counts as a catastrophic injury

- Traumatic brain injuries
- Spinal cord injuries and paralysis
- Amputations
- Severe burns
- Injuries that leave permanent disability or disfigurement

## Building a case around the rest of your life

The bills you have today are only part of it. A full claim looks at future surgeries and therapy, home changes, equipment, in-home care, and the income you can no longer earn. We work with your doctors and, when needed, outside experts to put real numbers on those needs.

> **Why medical bills matter so much.** In serious injury cases, health insurers, hospitals and government programs often have a right to be paid back from the recovery. Before founding the firm, Trey represented Georgia hospitals on reimbursement. Resolving those claims well can change how much reaches you and your family.

## How we work

- An attorney handles your case, never only a paralegal or case manager.
- If you can't come to us, we come to you.
- We prepare the case as if a jury will hear it.

## Questions

### Who will actually handle my case?

An attorney. At Avery Carnes, your case is handled by a lawyer, never only by a paralegal, case manager or intake rep. The firm takes a limited number of cases each year so every client gets personal attention.

### Can you come to me?

Yes. If you can't come to our office at Perimeter Center, we come to you. Tell us where you are when you call.

### What is my case worth?

No honest lawyer can give you a number on the first call. What a case is worth depends on the injuries, the medical treatment and bills, lost income, how the injury changes your life, who was at fault, and how much insurance is available. We'll explain each of those for your case and keep you updated as the facts come in.

### What changed in Georgia injury law in 2025?

Georgia passed a major tort reform law, Senate Bill 68, signed on April 21, 2025. For injuries on or after that date, the defense may show the jury whether you wore a seat belt, and what was actually paid, or is needed to pay, your medical bills, not just what was billed. It also limits how lawyers can suggest dollar amounts for pain and suffering, and in most cases lets either side require a trial to be split into a fault phase and a damages phase. These rules make careful handling of medical bills and evidence more important than ever.

# Atlanta Slip and Fall Lawyer

Stores, apartment complexes and other businesses have to keep their property reasonably safe. When they ignore a hazard and someone gets hurt, they can be responsible.

## Georgia at a glance

- **O.C.G.A. § 51-3-1**: owners must use ordinary care to keep premises safe for invited guests
- **Video**: store cameras are often recorded over, so ask for footage fast
- **2 years**: to file most injury lawsuits in Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33)

## What Georgia law requires of property owners

Under O.C.G.A. § 51-3-1, an owner or occupier must use ordinary care to keep the premises and approaches safe for people invited onto the property, like customers and tenants. In most fall cases you have to show the owner knew or should have known about the hazard, and you did not.

## Common causes

- Spills and wet floors with no warning
- Broken stairs, missing handrails, uneven walkways
- Poor lighting in parking decks and stairwells
- Ice, leaks and drainage problems

## What to do now

1. Report the fall to the manager and ask for a copy of the incident report.
2. Take photos of what made you fall, before it's cleaned up or fixed.
3. Get names and numbers of witnesses.
4. Get medical care, and call us so we can ask for camera footage quickly.

## Questions

### What if I was partly at fault?

Georgia uses a modified comparative fault rule (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33). You can still recover if you were less than 50% at fault, but your award is reduced by your share of the fault. At 50% or more, you recover nothing. Insurers know this, which is why they often try to shift blame onto the injured person.

### How long do I have to file an injury claim in Georgia?

For most injury claims, Georgia gives you **two years from the date of the injury** to file a lawsuit (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33). Claims against a government are much shorter: written notice to a city is due within **six months** (O.C.G.A. § 36-33-5), and to a county or the State within **twelve months** (O.C.G.A. § 36-11-1 and § 50-21-26). Miss the deadline and the claim can be lost for good.

### How much does it cost to hire Avery Carnes?

Your first consultation is free. We take injury cases on a contingency fee, which means **no attorney's fee unless we recover money for you**. The fee is a percentage of the recovery, set out in a written agreement you sign before we start. That agreement also explains how case costs, like filing fees and expert fees, are handled.

### What is my case worth?

No honest lawyer can give you a number on the first call. What a case is worth depends on the injuries, the medical treatment and bills, lost income, how the injury changes your life, who was at fault, and how much insurance is available. We'll explain each of those for your case and keep you updated as the facts come in.

Miss the deadline and the claim can be lost for good.

### Should I give a statement to the other driver's insurance company?

You do not have to give a recorded statement to the other driver's insurer, and it is usually smart to talk to a lawyer first. Their adjuster's job is to pay as little as possible. Your own policy may require you to cooperate with your own insurer, so read it or ask us.

# Gwinnett County Personal Injury Lawyer

Ben Avery grew up in Gwinnett County and graduated from Buford High School. Today he and Trey represent people hurt across Gwinnett, from Buford to Snellville.

## Gwinnett County at a glance

- **Courts**: Gwinnett Justice and Administration Center, 75 Langley Dr., Lawrenceville
- **Home county**: Ben grew up here and graduated from Buford High School
- **Notice**: claims against a city need written notice within 6 months (O.C.G.A. § 36-33-5)

## Communities we serve

Lawrenceville, Duluth, Snellville, Norcross, Suwanee, Buford, Lilburn, Peachtree Corners

Main roads where we see crashes: I-85, GA-316, I-985, Peachtree Industrial Boulevard, Pleasant Hill Road.

## Injury cases we handle in Gwinnett County

Crashes on I-85, GA-316 and I-985, and on busy roads like Peachtree Industrial Boulevard and Pleasant Hill Road. Truck crashes along the I-85 freight corridor. Falls, dog bites, nursing home neglect and wrongful death.

## Where a Gwinnett County case is heard

Most injury lawsuits here are filed in the State Court or Superior Court of Gwinnett County, at the Gwinnett Justice and Administration Center, 75 Langley Dr., Lawrenceville.

## Deadlines to watch

Most injury claims must be filed within two years (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33). For claims against a city, written notice is due within **six months** (O.C.G.A. § 36-33-5). Gwinnett County gets **twelve months** (O.C.G.A. § 36-11-1).

## Questions

### How long do I have to file an injury claim in Georgia?

For most injury claims, Georgia gives you **two years from the date of the injury** to file a lawsuit (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33). Claims against a government are much shorter: written notice to a city is due within **six months** (O.C.G.A. § 36-33-5), and to a county or the State within **twelve months** (O.C.G.A. § 36-11-1 and § 50-21-26). Miss the deadline and the claim can be lost for good.

### What if I was partly at fault?

Georgia uses a modified comparative fault rule (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33). You can still recover if you were less than 50% at fault, but your award is reduced by your share of the fault. At 50% or more, you recover nothing. Insurers know this, which is why they often try to shift blame onto the injured person.

### Can you come to me?

Yes. If you can't come to our office at Perimeter Center, we come to you. Tell us where you are when you call.

### How much does it cost to hire Avery Carnes?

Your first consultation is free. We take injury cases on a contingency fee, which means **no attorney's fee unless we recover money for you**. The fee is a percentage of the recovery, set out in a written agreement you sign before we start. That agreement also explains how case costs, like filing fees and expert fees, are handled.

## Cobb County at a glance

## Communities we serve

Marietta, Smyrna, Kennesaw, Acworth, Powder Springs, Austell, Mableton

Main roads where we see crashes: I-75, I-285 at Cumberland, I-575, Cobb Parkway (US-41), Windy Hill Road.

## Injury cases we handle in Cobb County

Crashes on I-75, I-575 and I-285 around Cumberland, and on Cobb Parkway and Windy Hill Road. Truck crashes, motorcycle crashes, falls, dog bites and wrongful death.

Many people hurt in Cobb are treated at Wellstar Kennestone Hospital in Marietta. Wherever you were treated, keep every bill and record.

## Where a Cobb County case is heard

Injury lawsuits here are usually filed in the State Court of Cobb County (12 East Park Square, Marietta) or Cobb County Superior Court (70 Haynes St., Marietta).

## Deadlines to watch

Most injury claims must be filed within two years (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33). For claims against a city, like Marietta or Smyrna, written notice is due within **six months** (O.C.G.A. § 36-33-5). Cobb County gets **twelve months** (O.C.G.A. § 36-11-1).

## Questions

### How long do I have to file an injury claim in Georgia?

For most injury claims, Georgia gives you **two years from the date of the injury** to file a lawsuit (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33). Claims against a government are much shorter: written notice to a city is due within **six months** (O.C.G.A. § 36-33-5), and to a county or the State within **twelve months** (O.C.G.A. § 36-11-1 and § 50-21-26). Miss the deadline and the claim can be lost for good.

### Should I give a statement to the other driver's insurance company?

You do not have to give a recorded statement to the other driver's insurer, and it is usually smart to talk to a lawyer first. Their adjuster's job is to pay as little as possible. Your own policy may require you to cooperate with your own insurer, so read it or ask us.

### What if I was partly at fault?

Georgia uses a modified comparative fault rule (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33). You can still recover if you were less than 50% at fault, but your award is reduced by your share of the fault. At 50% or more, you recover nothing. Insurers know this, which is why they often try to shift blame onto the injured person.

### How much does it cost to hire Avery Carnes?

Your first consultation is free. We take injury cases on a contingency fee, which means **no attorney's fee unless we recover money for you**. The fee is a percentage of the recovery, set out in a written agreement you sign before we start. That agreement also explains how case costs, like filing fees and expert fees, are handled.

# Georgia injury questions, answered

### How much does it cost to hire Avery Carnes?

Your first consultation is free. We take injury cases on a contingency fee, which means **no attorney's fee unless we recover money for you**. The fee is a percentage of the recovery, set out in a written agreement you sign before we start. That agreement also explains how case costs, like filing fees and expert fees, are handled.

### How long do I have to file an injury claim in Georgia?

For most injury claims, Georgia gives you **two years from the date of the injury** to file a lawsuit (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33). Claims against a government are much shorter: written notice to a city is due within **six months** (O.C.G.A. § 36-33-5), and to a county or the State within **twelve months** (O.C.G.A. § 36-11-1 and § 50-21-26). Miss the deadline and the claim can be lost for good.

### What if I was partly at fault?

Georgia uses a modified comparative fault rule (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33). You can still recover if you were less than 50% at fault, but your award is reduced by your share of the fault. At 50% or more, you recover nothing. Insurers know this, which is why they often try to shift blame onto the injured person.

### Should I give a statement to the other driver's insurance company?

You do not have to give a recorded statement to the other driver's insurer, and it is usually smart to talk to a lawyer first. Their adjuster's job is to pay as little as possible. Your own policy may require you to cooperate with your own insurer, so read it or ask us.

### Who will actually handle my case?

An attorney. At Avery Carnes, your case is handled by a lawyer, never only by a paralegal, case manager or intake rep. The firm takes a limited number of cases each year so every client gets personal attention.

### Can you come to me?

Yes. If you can't come to our office at Perimeter Center, we come to you. Tell us where you are when you call.

### What is my case worth?

No honest lawyer can give you a number on the first call. What a case is worth depends on the injuries, the medical treatment and bills, lost income, how the injury changes your life, who was at fault, and how much insurance is available. We'll explain each of those for your case and keep you updated as the facts come in.

### What changed in Georgia injury law in 2025?

Georgia passed a major tort reform law, Senate Bill 68, signed on April 21, 2025. For injuries on or after that date, the defense may show the jury whether you wore a seat belt, and what was actually paid, or is needed to pay, your medical bills, not just what was billed. It also limits how lawyers can suggest dollar amounts for pain and suffering, and in most cases lets either side require a trial to be split into a fault phase and a damages phase. These rules make careful handling of medical bills and evidence more important than ever.

### Where is your office?

We're in The King Building, 6 Concourse Pkwy #1650, Atlanta, GA 30328, at Perimeter Center near GA-400 and I-285. Call 404-602-0028.

### Which areas do you serve?

We represent injured people across metro Atlanta, including [Fulton County](https://avery-carnes.vercel.app/areas-we-serve/fulton-county/), [DeKalb County](https://avery-carnes.vercel.app/areas-we-serve/dekalb-county/), [Gwinnett County](https://avery-carnes.vercel.app/areas-we-serve/gwinnett-county/), [Cobb County](https://avery-carnes.vercel.app/areas-we-serve/cobb-county/) and [Sandy Springs](https://avery-carnes.vercel.app/areas-we-serve/sandy-springs/). The firm has represented clients in 25 Georgia counties.

### Will my case go to trial?

Many injury claims settle without a trial. Some don't, and insurers pay attention to which lawyers are ready to try a case. The firm has litigated in Georgia's state and federal courts, and Ben has tried cases to verdict.

### Does it cost anything to call?

No. The call and the case review are free, and there is no obligation to hire us.
